9820321b1a.q: How should CFOs distinguish between legitimate cost increases and billing leakage in freight expenses?
9820321b1a.a: Legitimate cost increases, such as correctly billed and owed tariffs, are not leakage—they are just increased costs to do business. Actual leakage shows up…
9820321b1a.e: The Man Who Finds Hidden Freight Costs | Oliver Nodjoumi  ICC Logistics
f: Legitimate cost increases—such as correctly billed tariffs and carrier rate hikes—are not leakage; they are simply higher costs to do business. Real leakage appears as missed billings, improperly applied charges, and inefficient routing , often disguised when multiple cost pressures hit simultaneously. CFOs must audit shipment profiles, routing efficiency, and actual carrier pricing to identify where leakage truly occurs.

The core confusion stems from timing. When tariffs rise, inflation climbs, and carrier prices increase all at once, CFOs face a perfect storm that masks billing errors. A 15% increase in freight costs might appear inevitable—when in reality, half of that could be undetected leakage.

Leakage takes specific forms. Warehouses that fail to measure and weigh items correctly cause shippers to be billed at higher rates than what appears on the manifest. As Oliver Najumi explains in the episode , this is where forensic-level auditing becomes essential. Incorrect dimensional weight classifications, missing surcharges that should have been applied to the bill (but weren't), and suboptimal routing all create cost leakage that compounds over time.
The three hidden sources of leakage

Missed billings occur when carriers fail to charge for services rendered—a benefit in the short term, but often a sign that your billing data is unreliable. More commonly, improperly applied charges show up when accessorial surcharges are applied inconsistently or when dimensional weight thresholds change without your routing strategy adjusting. Inefficient routing happens when shippers don't diversify carriers or don't consolidate shipments when it makes economic sense.

A practical example: if one customer's accessorial costs jumped $200,000 annually when weight and dimension thresholds changed, that shift alone can mask deeper issues in how shipments are being classified. The episode details how ICC Logistics processes roughly $9 billion per year of shipping cost transactional data , allowing them to spot patterns that individual shippers cannot detect alone.

e5469cbca7.q: What specific process should a logistics leader follow when brought in to protect freight margin over a 90-day period?
e5469cbca7.a: First, pull the most recent trailing 12 months of all data to understand the specific shipper's actual shipment profile and exposures. Then organize…
e5469cbca7.e: The Man Who Finds Hidden Freight Costs | Oliver Nodjoumi  ICC Logistics
f: The process begins by pulling the trailing 12 months of shipment data to map the shipper's actual profile and cost exposures. Next, organize internal routing principles to understand how the full provider portfolio is executed, then run this data against a data warehouse containing roughly $9 billion annually in shipping transactional data to identify what rates are truly competitive. The result is not a fixed budget, but a moving-target budget that adjusts as market conditions shift —protecting margin in real time rather than against an outdated projection.
Building the Foundation: Data, Routing, and Competitive Intelligence

The first step is forensic: collect a full 12 months of trailing data from the shipper's own transactions. This isn't a rough estimate or a category average—it's the real shipment history, including origin, destination, weight, dimensions, service level, and actual costs paid. Without this foundation, any margin protection strategy is built on guesswork.

Once you have the data, the second layer is internal routing analysis. Understanding how the organization currently executes its logistics—which carriers handle which lanes, what service commitments exist, where redundancy sits—reveals the true operational picture. As Oliver Najumi explains in the episode , this is where you discover whether the portfolio of logistics providers is being deployed logically or reactively.

The third and most decisive step is benchmarking against reality. Running the shipper's actual data against a data warehouse containing roughly $9 billion per year of shipping cost transactional data reveals exactly what is competitive in the market today and what is not. This isn't theoretical pricing—it's what real shippers actually pay in real transactions across carriers, lanes, and service types.
"There is no Bloomberg for freight, so it teaches you to be forensic in how you audit shipping operations."

45c330fb78.q: What are accessorial charges and how dramatically can they impact total shipping costs?
45c330fb78.a: Accessorials are simply surcharges applied to freight, fuel, and other shipping components. In small package shipping, they can be much more impactful. One…
45c330fb78.e: The Man Who Finds Hidden Freight Costs | Oliver Nodjoumi  ICC Logistics
f: Accessorial charges are surcharges layered onto freight costs for dimensions, weight, handling, and other special conditions. These fees can easily represent 47% of a company's total shipping spend —and they shift quietly, with one retailer facing a sudden $200,000 annual cost jump when weight and dimension thresholds changed overnight.
From $9 to $58.75: How a Single Surcharge Can Spiral

One furniture company's experience illustrates the scale of the problem. An accessorial charge for items over 48 inches or exceeding 40 pounds started at $9 in 2015. By 2024, that same charge had climbed to $58.75— a 582% increase over 11 years . This wasn't driven by inflation, which over the same period rose far more modestly. The charge compounded silently across thousands of shipments, invisible to many finance teams still budgeting off last year's baseline.

What makes accessorials particularly dangerous is that they're not negotiated upfront like base rates. As Oliver Najumi explains in the episode , carriers adjust these thresholds and fees with minimal transparency. When a 48-inch length limit suddenly becomes 42 inches, or when weight bands shift, exposure multiplies across entire SKU portfolios—sometimes overnight.
Why Accessorials Matter More Than the Headline Rate

Most CFOs benchmark shipping against inflation rates or carrier base-rate increases. That's a critical mistake. Accessorial fees often dwarf headline rate changes in their total impact. For the furniture customer mentioned above, nearly half of the $400,000 annual budget came from these surcharges alone, not from the stated freight rate.

946ecef4e2.q: Why do shipping cost increases consistently outpace inflation rates year over year?
946ecef4e2.a: Shipping rates increase at a much higher rate than inflation, averaging 6% a year across the board. Even when inflation is low, shipping costs consistently…
946ecef4e2.e: The Man Who Finds Hidden Freight Costs | Oliver Nodjoumi  ICC Logistics
f: Shipping rates increase an average of 6% per year , regardless of inflation levels—a pattern that has held steady for the past 25 years. Even when inflation drops, carrier rate increases continue relentlessly, compounding year after year into substantial margin erosion for shippers.
A Structural Problem That Inflation Cannot Explain

The fundamental issue is that inflation is a poor benchmark for freight budgets . While inflation measures the general rise in consumer prices across the economy, shipping rates operate under different pressures. Oliver Najumi of ICC Logistics explains that carriers raise rates as a structural business practice, independent of broader economic conditions.

This year, the pressure is intensifying. As discussed in the episode , peak season surcharges are stacking atop new rate increases from October through January 2027, creating compounding cost exposure that most CFOs fail to anticipate because they budget off outdated numbers.
The Accessorial Cost Trap

Beyond base rate increases, hidden fees—known as accessorials—amplify the true cost of shipping far beyond the headline rate. One customer discovered in their freight audit that when weight and dimension thresholds changed, their accessorial costs jumped by $200,000 annually . A furniture shipper found that nearly 47% of their entire $400,000 annual shipping budget was consumed by accessorial charges alone.

407c210a1d.q: What is the difference between a container that is cleared by customs and one that is physically movable in intermodal freight operations?
407c210a1d.a: A container can have its regulatory release and paperwork showing it as clear, but physically the container may still be buried in a stack or blocked by other equipment staged in the wrong place or otherwise inaccessible when a driver arrives. Cleared is a regulatory status, while movable is an operational readiness—the supply chain moves equipment, not documents.
f: Clearance by customs is purely a regulatory status documented on paper —it means the cargo has passed compliance checks. Physical movability is operational readiness: the container must actually be accessible, not buried in a stack or blocked by misplaced equipment at the terminal. The supply chain moves equipment, not documents.
This gap emerged as a core theme at the IANA Intermodal Expo 2026 , where supply chain leaders wrestled with a fundamental question: can freight actually move when the supply chain says it should?

A container with all clearances in place may still sit immobilized at a terminal because its physical location makes it inaccessible. Another piece of equipment, staged in the wrong position, can block an entire stack . A driver arrives to pick up a "cleared" container only to find it pinned behind other cargo. The paperwork says go; the yard says wait.

This distinction matters because it exposes a real operational risk. Shippers and carriers often track customs status as a proxy for readiness, but clearance alone guarantees nothing about actual pickup availability. Operational visibility—knowing where equipment sits and what blocks access—is the second half of the problem .
Cleared (Regulatory Status)
A container has satisfied CTPAT (Customs-Trade Partnership Against Terrorism) inspection and customs documentation. All compliance paperwork is complete. Movable (Operational Status)

6c04f0c1a5.q: How can trusted trade data and cargo information be used earlier in the terminal placement process to improve freight accessibility?
6c04f0c1a5.a: If a terminal shows that a container is low risk or already likely to be cleared, it may be able to position that box where it can be accessed more easily. This can reduce re-handles, improve dredge dispatch, improve chassis turns, and create more predictable ramp flows, while giving the shipper a more accurate answer to whether freight is actually available.
f: When terminals receive trusted trade data showing a container is low-risk or already cleared, they can position that cargo in accessible locations instead of burial stacks , reducing re-handles and improving dispatch efficiency. This early intelligence gives shippers accurate answers about freight availability and creates more predictable ramp flows.

The core challenge in intermodal operations is the gap between regulatory clearance and physical accessibility. A container can have its customs paperwork complete but still be physically blocked by other cargo in a terminal stack. Using trusted trade data earlier in the placement process means terminals can make smarter positioning decisions from the moment a container arrives.

This approach delivers multiple operational benefits. Fewer re-handles mean less equipment movement and lower handling costs. Improved dredge dispatch keeps rail operations running on schedule. Faster chassis turns reduce equipment sitting time. And predictable ramp flows allow trucking operations to plan pickups with confidence. The result is a supply chain where freight actually moves when it should move.

As discussed in the episode from the IANA Intermodal Expo 2026 , this capability depends on better visibility across the entire intermodal ecosystem—a conversation that brought together terminals, rail carriers, trucking providers, and technology firms all focused on the same operational friction point.

The shipper benefit is equally concrete. Instead of uncertain wait times, they receive a reliable answer about when freight is actually available for pickup. This predictability flows upstream into planning and downstream into customer commitments, making the entire supply chain more responsive to real demand.

Implementation requires terminals to trust the data sources they're receiving. Systems like CTPAT pre-clearance and customs collaboration agreements lower the risk profile of containers entering the supply chain. When that trusted signal is paired with real-time positioning intelligence, terminals can move from reactive stacking to proactive placement.

5d53e215cb.q: What preventative maintenance and inspection practices can reduce out-of-service violations in intermodal drayage operations?
5d53e215cb.a: Many out-of-service violations can be prevented before a truck leaves the yard. The industry needs a genuine inspection culture, which includes time for proper pre-trip training focused on real operating conditions, responsive maintenance, and incentives that reward prevention instead of treating on-time performance as the only measure that matters. The cheapest breakdown is the one identified before the truck leaves the yard.
f: Most out-of-service violations can be prevented before a truck ever leaves the yard. Building a genuine inspection culture —supported by proper pre-trip training tied to real operating conditions, responsive maintenance, and incentive structures that reward prevention—eliminates the cheapest breakdown of all: the one you catch before departure.

The key insight is structural: many freight operations still measure success almost exclusively by on-time performance, which inadvertently pushes drivers and dispatchers to defer or skip critical pre-trip inspections. A breakdown discovered in the yard costs time, but at least the truck hasn't left yet. A breakdown on the road creates a failed delivery, lost revenue, and regulatory violations.

Pre-trip training must be grounded in the actual conditions drivers face —not generic safety videos. This means training that reflects the weight distributions, terrain, weather patterns, and equipment configurations specific to a driver's regular routes. When drivers understand why they're inspecting specific components, they're more likely to perform those inspections consistently.

Responsive maintenance is equally critical. If a driver reports a steering issue or brake wear during a pre-trip, the maintenance team must be resourced to address it the same day. Delays between inspection and repair create a gap where a vehicle can leave the yard in unsafe condition. This is where real-world asset intelligence tools discussed at the IANA Intermodal Expo become operationally relevant—they flag problems before they become violations.

Incentive alignment is the final lever. Operations that reward both on-time performance and violation-free records see faster adoption of inspection discipline. When bonuses or performance metrics equally weight safety compliance alongside delivery speed, the yard inspection culture shifts from a box to check to a core operational practice.
The economics of early detection

b10c0f9b46.q: What specific operational problem did Union Pacific identify in the Norfolk Southern to Union Pacific corridor from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania to Salt Lake City?

A combined railroad would replace that lift, dray, and reload with a block swap in Chicago, projecting a 20-24-hour transit improvement.

d6d2e8da64.q: What does Oliver Wyman's 2025 shipper survey reveal about why shippers are shifting freight from rail to truck?

The survey also found that pricing is a critical modal decision factor and that shippers remain frustrated by the complexity and slow commercial response.

23b176bdfe.q: Why does a large global container fleet not guarantee available capacity on critical trade lanes?
23b176bdfe.a: Installed capacity is not the same as usable capacity. Ships waiting at congested ports become unavailable for the next voyage, vessels rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope take longer to complete rotations, and geopolitically disrupted ships cannot reposition containers or return to normal schedules. Blank sailings marketed to customers may never actually arrive, creating scarcity despite fleet size.
f: Installed capacity is not the same as usable capacity. Ships waiting at congested ports become unavailable for the next voyage , vessels rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope take longer to complete rotations, and geopolitically disrupted ships cannot reposition containers or return to normal schedules. Blank sailings marketed to customers may never actually arrive, creating acute scarcity despite record fleet size.
The Congestion and Rerouting Trap

Port congestion is not a temporary bottleneck—it actively removes vessels from productive service. When a container ship waits outside a congested port, it cannot start its next rotation on schedule. That delay cascades across the entire trade lane, effectively shrinking usable capacity even though the vessel still exists on paper.

Geopolitical disruptions have created a secondary availability problem. Vessels forced to reroute through the Cape of Good Hope instead of the Suez Canal add 10–14 days to their voyage time, reducing the number of completed rotations per year. Fewer rotations mean fewer slot opportunities for shippers, regardless of the global fleet size. A ship locked out of normal geography is a ship that cannot serve the market reliably.
Carrier Capacity Management and Blank Sailings

Carriers have actively withdrawn scheduled capacity across major east-west trades. In the first half of 2026, carriers withdrew 10–14% of scheduled capacity on Asia-to-U.S. and Asia-to-Europe lanes. This is a deliberate choice to support rate stability, not a result of ships being unavailable.

d08adf5bc4.q: What percentage of global container shipping capacity was constrained by port waiting times?
d08adf5bc4.a: Roughly 11% of global container ship capacity was waiting outside ports, with higher vessel arrival to berth times in North Europe and schedule reliability remaining well below pre-pandemic benchmarks. Container shipping operates as a tightly connected system where delays at one port create ripple effects throughout the entire freight network.
f: Roughly 11% of global container ship capacity was waiting outside ports , unable to load or discharge cargo. This bottleneck doesn't simply slow individual shipments—it cascades through the entire freight network, reducing the effective capacity available to shippers across all trade lanes and creating persistent delays that ripple far beyond the congested port itself.

Port congestion represents a structural constraint that most shippers underestimate. Ships sitting idle at anchor or in waiting zones are not available for their next voyage, and this idle time compounds across the network. According to the FreightFlow Advisor analysis , this congestion problem is especially acute in North Europe, where vessel arrival-to-berth times remain significantly elevated compared to pre-pandemic levels.

The practical implication is immediate: installed capacity—the number of ships in the global fleet—bears little relation to usable capacity. A vessel waiting three weeks for a berth slot is, for that period, offline. When carriers simultaneously withdraw 10-14% of scheduled capacity across major east-west trade lanes (reaching 14% on Asia-U.S. East Coast routes), the compounding effect is severe. Container shipping operates as a tightly connected system where delays at one port ripple throughout the entire freight network, affecting shippers across routes that should have no direct relationship to the congested port.

Schedule reliability, a metric measuring whether carriers meet their published arrival and departure times, remains well below pre-pandemic benchmarks across all major routes. This unreliability itself becomes a capacity constraint. The episode explores how reliability is not just a service metric—it is capacity . When shippers cannot rely on a vessel to arrive on time, they must plan for longer lead times and buffer stock, effectively reducing the usable capacity of the network.
Why installed capacity is not the same as available capacity

The distinction between total ship capacity and effective capacity has become central to understanding modern container shipping. Even with a record global order book representing approximately 37% of the existing fleet under construction, the market is not behaving as the simple logic would predict: more ships should mean lower rates. Yet rates have continued to rise in both spot and contract markets.

97064496b1.q: How have Red Sea diversions impacted vessel availability and service frequency?
97064496b1.a: Diversions around the Cape of Good Hope since late 2023 have added time, fuel consumption, and vessel days to Asia-Europe rotations. You need more ships to offer the same level of weekly service when each voyage takes longer, absorbing effective capacity.
f: Since late 2023, rerouting around the Red Sea via the Cape of Good Hope has extended Asia-Europe voyage times significantly , forcing carriers to deploy more ships to maintain the same weekly service frequency. Each voyage absorbs more vessel days, reducing the effective capacity available across the trade lane.

When a single rotation takes longer—adding time, fuel consumption, and operational complexity—the mathematics of capacity shift fundamentally. A carrier that previously cycled a ship through eight rotations per year now completes only six or seven. To sustain a weekly service commitment with fewer annual rotations per vessel, they must add ships to the fleet rotation, even if the total global fleet size remains unchanged.

This dynamic reveals why the FreightFlow Advisor team explains in their episode that installed capacity—the number of ships that exist—differs fundamentally from usable capacity. A ship delayed by port congestion, rerouted by geopolitical disruption, or waiting outside a bottlenecked terminal is unavailable for its next scheduled sailing. That gap between theoretical and practical capacity is where rate pressure now emerges.

The impact cascades across contract rates. According to data discussed on the podcast , long-term contract rates on Asia to U.S. West Coast and East Coast lanes climbed 41% and 40% respectively in the first half of 2026—far outpacing the 6% spot rate movement to $6,244 per 40-foot container. This divergence signals that carriers are tightening their capacity commitments, not loosening them, despite an order book representing approximately 37% of the existing global fleet.

Effective capacity: The portion of available ships actively sailing and meeting service schedules on a given trade lane, distinguished from installed capacity (total ships in existence). Effective capacity shrinks when vessels are delayed at ports, rerouted around geopolitical hotspots, or held in reserve as carriers manage demand strategically.

The Red Sea rerouting also coincides with carriers actively withdrawing scheduled capacity across major east-west trades. This strategic withdrawal, explored in detail on the podcast , reflects how carriers are managing supply tighter than supply-side metrics suggest they should—a signal that the bottleneck is not ship availability in absolute terms, but how many ships can reliably reach destination on time.

9356a124f3.q: To what extent are carriers reducing scheduled capacity across major east-west trade lanes?
9356a124f3.a: Carriers withdrew between 10 and 14 percent of scheduled capacity across four major east-west trades in the first half of 2026. Asia to U.S. East Coast had the highest withdrawal at 14 percent, followed by Asia to U.S. West Coast and Asia to North Europe at 11 percent each, and Asia to Mediterranean at 10 percent.
f: Carriers withdrew 10 to 14 percent of scheduled capacity across four major east-west trade lanes in the first half of 2026. Asia to U.S. East Coast experienced the steepest cut at 14 percent, while Asia to U.S. West Coast and Asia to North Europe each saw 11 percent withdrawals, and Asia to Mediterranean declined by 10 percent.
Capacity Management in a Congested Market

This capacity withdrawal is not simply a response to weak demand. Instead, it reflects a deliberate strategy by carriers to align scheduled capacity with what they can reliably operate given persistent port congestion and geopolitical disruptions. When ships spend extra time waiting at congested ports or rerouting around blocked passages like the Red Sea, fewer vessels become available for scheduled rotations—even though the total fleet size continues to grow.

The data from Lodestar, as discussed in the episode , shows the gap between installed capacity and effective capacity widening. According to the same analysis, approximately 11 percent of global container ship capacity was waiting outside ports , further shrinking the pool of ships available to move cargo on schedule.

This dynamic explains why Asia to U.S. East Coast—the trade lane most exposed to Red Sea diversions around the Cape of Good Hope—saw the largest withdrawal. Vessels need more calendar days to complete each rotation when they take the longer route, which compresses the number of round trips a ship can make in a given period. Carriers respond by reducing their published schedule rather than promising reliability they cannot keep.
Why Carriers Are Pulling Scheduled Capacity, Not Just Pricing

dfed48ff29.q: What recent rate movements signal that pressure is shifting from spot markets to contract rates?
dfed48ff29.a: According to Lodestar, Asia to Los Angeles spot rates rose 6% to $6,244 per 40-foot container. More significantly, average long-term rates on Asia to U.S. West Coast and East Coast trades were up 41% and 40% respectively, indicating carriers believe disruption is durable enough to reprice longer-term commitments.
f: Long-term contract rates on Asia-to-U.S. routes jumped 40-41% while spot rates rose only 6% , signaling that carriers now believe supply disruptions are durable enough to reprice longer-term commitments. This rate divergence marks a fundamental shift from the traditional pattern where spot rates move first while contract rates lag.

Spot rates move quickly, responding to immediate demand, available vessel space, and port conditions. Contract rates, by contrast, are meant to provide stability—a shipper commits volume and a carrier commits capacity over a defined period. Typically, spot rates fluctuate first while contract rates follow slowly or lag significantly behind. The current market is breaking this pattern , as detailed in The FreightFA Brief Podcast .
The divergence signals carrier confidence in sustained disruption

When carriers reprice long-term contracts upward by 40 percent or more, they are making a explicit bet that current supply constraints will persist. According to data from Lodestar, Asia to Los Angeles spot rates rose 6% to $6,244 per 40-foot container—a meaningful increase on its own, but dwarfed by the average long-term rate movements: 41% on Asia to U.S. West Coast trades and 40% on Asia to U.S. East Coast trades .

This repricing reflects carriers' assessment that the traditional economic forces driving freight markets have shifted. Rather than the conventional assumption that "more ships mean cheaper freight," the market is now pricing in the reality that effective capacity remains constrained by congestion and geopolitical disruption , not by the absolute number of vessels in the global fleet.

For shippers locked into spot market purchases, this divergence creates urgency. The episode explores how carriers are managing capacity strategically to maintain pricing power even as new vessel orders swell the future fleet. The lag between spot and contract rate movements, once a buffer that gave shippers time to assess market direction, is narrowing—and carriers are signaling they do not expect relief soon.

aeb7910305.q: How should freight operators evaluate carrier and forwarder performance beyond rate negotiations?
aeb7910305.a: Shippers should separate rate risk from service risk by asking about actual schedule performance, what happens if a vessel skips the port, where empties come from, fallback gateway options, and how surcharges are governed. Missing sailings, late transshipments, poor equipment cycles, and delayed inland handoffs can be more expensive than rate increases and are often harder to see in time.
f: Freight operators must separate rate risk from service risk by evaluating actual schedule performance, port skip contingencies, empty equipment sourcing, fallback gateway options, and surcharge governance —not just contract rates. Missing sailings, late transshipments, poor equipment cycles, and delayed inland handoffs can cost more than rate increases and are far harder to detect in time.
The Hidden Cost of Service Failure

When a vessel skips a port or a transshipment runs late, the cost compounds across your entire supply chain. Yet these failures often go unmeasured because shippers focus primarily on the negotiated rate. An equipment cycle that stretches longer than planned or an inland handoff that misses your window can disrupt production schedules and tie up working capital in ways that a 5% or 10% rate increase never would.

This is where the FreightFlow Advisor team explains the real problem : operators focus their contracts on the variables they can negotiate—price—and ignore the variables that actually move the needle on total cost of service. The result is that a carrier or forwarder can deliver rate concessions while quietly degrading reliability in ways your negotiating team never sees until it's too late.
What to Ask Your Carriers and Forwarders

Begin with schedule integrity. Ask what percentage of sailings actually depart as published in the last 12 months, and what happens when a vessel skips your port—is there a guaranteed next sailing, or do you fall into a spot market auction? That transparency matters more than the rate card.

96d88e45c9.q: What contract provisions should address disruption in volatile ocean shipping environments?
96d88e45c9.a: Every significant ocean agreement should address routing changes, emergency surcharges, notice periods, force majeure, service failures, allocation treatment, and handling of cargo already in transit. Most contracts are written for normal conditions, but freight teams need them to work under abnormal conditions.
f: Every ocean freight contract must explicitly cover seven critical areas: routing changes, emergency surcharges, notice periods, force majeure, service failures, allocation treatment, and cargo already in transit. Most agreements are written for stable conditions—but freight teams need them to actually function when disruptions strike.
Why Standard Contracts Break Under Stress

The ocean freight market has shifted fundamentally. Effective capacity is now constrained by congestion and geopolitical disruption , not by the total number of ships available. When a vessel skips a port, gets rerouted around Africa, or sits idle waiting for dock space, shippers need explicit contract language telling them exactly what happens next.

Carriers have withdrawn between 10 and 14 percent of scheduled capacity across major east-west trades in 2026. In this environment, a vague contract creates chaos. As discussed in this episode of The FreightFA Brief Podcast , reliability has become a capacity problem—and that changes everything about how you negotiate protection.
The Seven Provisions Every Contract Needs

Routing and diversion rights must specify not just acceptable alternate routes, but what happens when a carrier chooses an unexpected path. If a vessel is rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope or Strait of Hormuz instead of the Red Sea, does the shipper absorb the cost or delay? The contract must say.

03eb515d50.q: How do sourcing diversification decisions create logistics network exposure?
03eb515d50.a: As companies diversify manufacturing beyond China to countries like Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand, Cambodia, India, and Mexico, they reshape where freight risk sits. Diversifying sourcing without diversifying logistics creates new exposure, especially where congestion challenges and loading delays at developing Southeast Asian ports are material.
f: When manufacturers move production to Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand, Cambodia, India, or Mexico to escape China-dependent supply chains, they reallocate manufacturing risk — but diversifying sourcing without diversifying logistics simply shifts freight risk to ports that lack the infrastructure to handle it . The result: congestion, loading delays, and material cost exposure precisely where companies expected cost relief.

The logic appears sound on paper. Spread suppliers across multiple countries, and you reduce dependency on any single geography or geopolitical flashpoint. But as explored in The FreightFA Brief Podcast , most companies execute only half the strategy. They diversify manufacturing but continue routing all freight through the same logistics corridors — often the congested Southeast Asian ports already under pressure.

Developing ports in Vietnam, Thailand, and Indonesia face material congestion challenges and loading delays that developed hubs like Singapore or Hong Kong do not. When a shipper fragments sourcing across five countries but funnels all consolidation through a single, understaffed Thai port, that port becomes the bottleneck. The purchasing department saved money on labor costs. The supply chain department absorbed it as schedule risk and premium rates.

A deeper layer compounds the problem. According to market data covered in the episode , approximately 11% of global container ship capacity sits idle outside ports , waiting to discharge or load. That capacity exists, but it is not available where shippers actually need it. A vessel delayed at a congested Southeast Asian port does not reduce overall capacity — it removes reliable capacity from the lanes shippers depend on. Reliability, in freight terms, is capacity.

Logistics Diversification means routing sourced freight through multiple ports, carriers, and corridors — not just multiple factories. A shipper sourcing from Vietnam and Thailand should consolidate through both Bangkok and Ho Chi Minh City ports, or add a non-congested third hub, rather than forcing all volume through a single gateway. The financial consequence is immediate. Carriers managing capacity across routes where 10–14% of scheduled sailings were cancelled in the first half of 2026 (as they were across Asia-to-U.S. East Coast and West Coast lanes) prioritize reliable customers with predictable volume patterns. Shippers whose freight arrives in bursts at already-congested ports rank lower in allocation. Premium charges follow, alongside longer transit times and reduced visibility into when freight will actually move.

The episode also details how contract rates on Asia-to-U.S. routes have risen 40–41% in parallel with spot rate pressure , signaling that shippers can no longer rely on negotiated agreements to insulate them from volatility. This amplifies the risk: a shipper with fragmented sourcing at a congested port has no fallback capacity and faces renegotiation on every renewal.
